title: Security deviation approval catalog and SIEM export guide
body:
Purpose:
This document provides a single-runbook catalog for approving security deviations (exceptions) during release windows, plus precise guidance for mapping audit log fields to our SIEM ingestion format. It is intended for release engineers, security reviewers, and SREs who must triage, approve, or audit temporary deviations to RBAC, network egress rules, or logging controls.

When to use this catalog:
- Emergency hotfix drives the team to temporarily relax a policy (e.g., open SSH to a diagnostic host).
- Planned rollout requires a temporary role override for a contractor or vendor.
- Backwards-incompatible RBAC v2 transition step requires granting legacy permissions during migration.
- Any production change that cannot meet the standard security gate within the planned release window.

Principles and SLAs:
- Exceptions are timeboxed: default max duration 72 hours unless explicitly approved for longer.
- Least privilege: scope changes must be as narrow as possible (role, resource, time).
- Evidence-first approvals: request must attach concrete evidence as described below.
- Approvals require 2 approvers for high-risk deviations (see risk matrix). Low-risk deviations may be approved by one security engineer + release owner.

Deviation request template (copy into Jira ticket):
- Summary: short title and impacted system
- Owner: service owner (name, pager, team)
- Requested change: exact RBAC change or rule to be relaxed (example: add role debug_readonly to service-A cluster X for 48h)
- Justification: why change is needed, expected outcome, rollback plan
- Scope: list resources (cluster, namespace, model-id, route id), accounts, and IP ranges
- Timebox: start and end timestamps (UTC)
- Evidence attached: runbook, diagnostic logs, test checklist, canary plan
- Risk classification: low | medium | high (see matrix)
- Approvers requested: security lead + release owner + infra lead (auto-populate by workflow)

Required evidence checklist (attach to request):
- Repro steps and exact commands used to enact the change
- Small-scale dry-run results (if applicable) with logs
- Planned verification checklist (what success looks like)
- Rollback playbook with precise commands and criteria for rollback
- Audit capture validation: example log lines showing the modification event
- SIEM forwarding test: proof that audit event arrives in SIEM with expected fields

RBAC v2 considerations (what reviewers look for):
- Role scoping: confirm the role being granted does not include excessive verbs (e.g., wildcards).
- Transitive effects: enumerate any service accounts that will inherit the new role.
- Token lifetime: if JWTs or short-lived tokens are reissued, confirm TTL complies with exception timebox.
- Temporary vs permanent flags: request must set a temporary flag that triggers automatic revocation.
- Policy sources: point to the policy id/version in the policy repo (example: policy repo SHA or PR).

Risk classification quick matrix (examples):
- Low: read-only access to non-sensitive telemetry, short-lived, single service owner approval.
- Medium: write access to non-customer data, cross-cluster permission, requires security + infra approval.
- High: access to customer PII, key management, ability to modify audit settings or disable logging—requires security lead + product security + exec approval.

Audit log schema mapping (what to capture for each approval event):
The following fields must be present in the audit record for any approved deviation. These map directly to our SIEM ingestion schema (field names after ->). Show example lines in the body for reviewer to validate.
- event_id -> event_id (UUID)
- timestamp -> @timestamp (ISO8601 UTC)
- actor -> user.id (email or service account)
- action -> event.action (e.g., rbac.grant, rbac.revoke)
- target_resource -> resource.id (cluster/namespace/service)
- change_blob -> change.details (JSON string with before/after where feasible)
- reason -> request.reason (short justification)
- request_ticket -> trace.ticket_id (Jira or ticket id)
- duration -> request.timebox_seconds (integer)
- approvers -> approvals.list (array of approver ids)
- evidence_links -> evidence.urls (array)

Example audit line (raw text log to validate ingestion):
{"@timestamp":"2026-03-09T18:22:13Z","event_id":"3b9f4a2e-7f3a-4c2b-b1f2-9e3f9d2f4aab","user.id":"alice@redwood.ai","event.action":"rbac.grant","resource.id":"cluster:prod-eu:service-A","change.details":"{\"added_roles\":[\"debug_readonly\"]}","trace.ticket_id":"SEC-4123","request.timebox_seconds":86400,"approvals.list":["maya.chen","diego.alvarez"],"evidence.urls":["https://confluence.redwood-inference.internal/pages/DEV-4563"]}

SIEM export & ingestion checklist:
- Export format: newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON), UTF-8, gzip compressed for batch uploads.
- Required fields: @timestamp, event_id, user.id, event.action, resource.id, change.details, trace.ticket_id. Missing required fields must cause the ingestion pipeline to tag the event as malformed and route to the security backlog.
- Field mapping and parsers: ensure change.details is stored as a string and parsed into nested fields in the SIEM only after validation. Avoid unvalidated JSON expansion to prevent field count explosion.
- Tagging: add tags.environment (prod|staging|dev), tags.risk (low|medium|high), tags.exception_timebox_days (integer).
- Liveness test: every exception approval must be followed by a SIEM ingestion test event (use the test endpoint /ingest-test) and attach the SIEM event id to the Jira ticket.

Approval workflow & automation hints:
- Automation: a Jira workflow transition sets a temporary flag in policy engine (policy-engine/api/temp-override) and triggers a policy-engine event. That event must write an audit log before making the runtime change.
- Auto-expiry: policy-engine must revoke the override at TTL expiry; revoke events must be recorded in the same audit schema.
- Escalation: if auto-revoke fails, the system opens SEC-ESCALATION and pages the on-call security SRE.

Sign-off stub (copy into ticket comments for final sign-off):
I, <approver name>, approve the requested deviation: <summary>. I have verified the evidence and SIEM ingestion example attached. I acknowledge the timebox of <hours> and commit to the rollback plan as documented.
Approver: <name>
Role: <security | infra | product>
Signed at: <UTC timestamp>

Post-launch monitoring (minimum):
- Hourly checks for first 6 hours, then 4-hour cadence until expiry.
- Confirm expected invocation pattern and no spike in error rates for affected services.
- Verify no unexpected privilege escalations or new principals in ACL lists.
- Attach monitoring snapshots (grafana links, flamegraphs, API call counts) to the ticket at 6h and at revoke.

Rollback triggers (examples):
- Canary failure (error rate > 3x baseline for 15m)
- Unauthorized access observed in SIEM or manual audit
- Auto-revoke failed and manual revoke cannot be completed in 30 minutes

Appendix: quick links and snippets:
- Policy engine temporary override API: POST https://policy-engine.redwood-inference.internal/api/v1/overrides
- SIEM test ingest endpoint: https://siem.redwood-inference.internal/ingest-test
- Example curl to create audit event: curl -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"@timestamp":"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)","event_id":"$(uuidgen)","user.id":"<me>","event.action":"rbac.grant","resource.id":"cluster:prod:service-A","change.details":"{"added_roles":["debug_readonly"]}","trace.ticket_id":"SEC-4123"}' https://audit-proxy.redwood-inference.internal/events

Notes to reviewers (informal):
- If you see a request that wants to "disable logging" or "suppress audit", treat it as high risk and require exec-level justification.
- Be skeptical of one-off SSH access requests; prefer ephemeral jump hosts instrumented by session recording.
- Keep the ticket comments concise; use the checklist above to validate quickly.

Revision history:
- 2025-10-21: initial draft (Maya Chen)
- 2025-12-05: added SIEM mapping and sample event (Diego Alvarez)
- 2026-03-10: clarified RBAC v2 transient token guidance and updated example formats (Priya Nair)
